abstract: Long-term memory depends upon the translation of the plasticity-related proteins required for synaptic consolidation. Whether learning-related changes in hippocampal CA1 coding and synchrony require local synaptic consolidation or reflect plasticity elsewhere remains unknown. We used the inducible protein kinase R (iPKR) chemogenetic system to downregulate cap-dependent translation in CaMKII-expressing dorsal CA1 neurons through intracerebral infusion of an actuator that activates the integrated stress response. Without chemogenetic activation, iPKR mice exhibited elevated pyramidal cell firing and reduced interneuron firing relative to wild-type mice. Infusion of the chemogenetic actuator suppressed c-Fos expression for at least 24 hours and blocked the novelty-related increase in firing observed following vehicle infusion. Nevertheless, other aspects of experience-dependent physiology persisted. Pyramidal cells active during novel exploration remained preferentially recruited into sharp-wave ripples (SPW-Rs) hours into a post-exposure consolidation period. Pairwise coincident activity patterns formed during novel exploration were also reactivated during SPW-Rs with magnitudes and temporal persistence comparable to vehicle sessions and wild-type mice without infusions. When mice returned five hours after exposure to a novel environment, the assemblies formed during translation disruption were also re-expressed at magnitudes comparable to those observed during repeated familiar-environment visits and following novel exploration under vehicle. These findings demonstrate that experience-dependent reorganization of CA1 pyramidal cell synchrony can survive disruption of plasticity-related protein production, whereas novelty-related changes in excitability are impaired. Therefore, SPW-R reactivation and cell assembly consolidation likely depend upon plasticity pathways outside of the eIF2-dependent signaling pathways in the CA1 pyramidal cells targeted by the iPKR system.
